name: Carcinoid Syndrome

ethnicAssociations: African American (slightly higher incidence of GI carcinoids)

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Clinical and biochemical criteria for carcinoid syndrome

criteria.description: Hepatic metastases (syndrome typically develops only after hepatic metastasis for GI carcinoids)
Positive somatostatin receptor scintigraphy (OctreoScan) or 68Ga-DOTATATE PET

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Clinical symptoms of carcinoid syndrome plus elevated 5-HIAA, with histologically confirmed neuroendocrine tumor
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Carcinoid syndrome occurs in <10% of patients with carcinoid tumors, usually requiring hepatic metastases to bypass first-pass hepatic metabolism of serotonin.

pathognomonic.notes: Typically face and upper trunk; can be triggered by alcohol, stress, exercise
Watery, non-bloody; due to serotonin-mediated increased gut motility

common.notes: Develop over time from chronic flushing episodes

occasional.notes: Tricuspid regurgitation and pulmonary stenosis; due to serotonin-mediated endocardial fibrosis
Due to tryptophan diversion to serotonin synthesis

rare.notes: Can occur during anesthesia or tumor manipulation; medical emergency
Seen with bronchial carcinoids or patent foramen ovale

laboratory: Elevated serum chromogranin A (nonspecific but useful for monitoring)
NT-proBNP elevation if carcinoid heart disease present
imaging: CT abdomen/pelvis showing primary tumor (most commonly ileal) and hepatic metastases
68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT (highest sensitivity for somatostatin receptor-positive NETs)
Echocardiography for carcinoid heart disease screening (tricuspid and pulmonary valve thickening)
MRI liver for hepatic metastases characterization
genetic: MEN1 gene mutations in some gastric and pancreatic NETs
Germline testing not routinely recommended unless syndromic features present
other: Tumor biopsy with chromogranin A, synaptophysin, Ki-67 staining
WHO grading based on Ki-67 index and mitotic rate
Provocative tests (pentagastrin stimulation) rarely used now

distinguishingFeatures: Pheochromocytoma features pallor rather than flushing
Bone marrow biopsy diagnostic for mastocytosis
Menopausal flushing associated with elevated FSH/LH
No diarrhea or wheezing in menopause

redFlags: Carcinoid crisis during surgery or anesthesia (treat with IV octreotide)
Progressive right-sided heart failure (carcinoid heart disease)
Rapidly progressive symptoms suggesting high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma
Mesenteric fibrosis causing bowel ischemia or obstruction
Severe pellagra-like dermatitis indicating advanced tryptophan depletion
references: Halperin DM, et al. Frequency of carcinoid syndrome at neuroendocrine tumour diagnosis. Lancet Oncol. 2017;18(4):525-534.
Modlin IM, et al. Current status of gastrointestinal carcinoids. Gastroenterology. 2005;128(6):1717-51.
Rubin de Celis Ferrari AC, et al. Carcinoid syndrome: update on the pathophysiology and treatment. Clinics. 2018;73(suppl 1):e490s.
Davar J, et al. Diagnosing and managing carcinoid heart disease. Cardiology. 2017;137(3):146-156.
